fixes.explanation: Right on, baker. The Teacher says "When good things increase, so do those who consume them…" (Ecclesiastes 5:11). The more that comes in, the more consumers show up to use it. I've watched a cookie box do this with my own eyes.

That's the reason the Teacher gives. He says "…one official is watched by a superior, and others higher still are over them." (Ecclesiastes 5:8) So one official has a superior watching, and others are higher still. I think that's his way of saying: don't fall over in shock when you see this, friend.

The Teacher never says the poor will rise up. He says one official is watched by a superior, and others higher still are over them (Ecclesiastes 5:8). That's his reason for not being astonished. An uprising isn't part of that reason.

Good guess, but the verse doesn't mention the king judging anybody. It says one official is watched by a superior, and others higher still are over them (Ecclesiastes 5:8). That is the reason he gives. A king does show up in the very next verse, but there he profits from the fields, and judging isn't mentioned (Ecclesiastes 5:9).

That's the word. "He who loves money is never satisfied by money…" (Ecclesiastes 5:10) It's like finishing a whole batch of cookies and still hunting the cooling rack for one more, friend. Having plenty and still wanting more is the whole picture.

Envy makes sense, but the Teacher doesn't say it. He says "When good things increase, so do those who consume them…" (Ecclesiastes 5:11). So the ones who increase are the ones who consume. Envy doesn't come up in the verse.

That's it. The Teacher asks "what then is the profit to the owner, except to behold them with his eyes?" (Ecclesiastes 5:11) All that stuff, and the owner's profit is looking at it. That's like baking twelve dozen cookies and getting to stand there and stare.

Nice thought, but bread isn't in this verse. The Teacher says the worker's sleep is sweet, while the abundance of the rich man permits him no sleep (Ecclesiastes 5:12). The comparison is about rest, not what's on the table. One man has sweet sleep and the other has none.

That's the one. The Teacher says "…all his days he eats in darkness, with much sorrow, sickness, and anger." (Ecclesiastes 5:17) I think this one hurts, friend. It's a heavy way to live, and it's the man who toils for the wind.

It's actually true. The Teacher says "…the few days of life that God has given him…" (Ecclesiastes 5:18). Few is his word for those days. It's right there in the verse, so True was the answer to pick.

Hoard doesn't fit. In this verse, God enables a man to enjoy his riches and wealth (Ecclesiastes 5:19). The word the verse gives is enjoy. Earlier the Teacher called "wealth hoarded to the harm of its owner…" a grievous evil (Ecclesiastes 5:13).

Count isn't the word the verse uses. God "…has enabled him to enjoy them, to accept his lot, and to rejoice in his labor." (Ecclesiastes 5:19) The word that fits is enjoy. You can count crumbs all day, friend, and still not taste the cookie.

Counting wealth isn't the reason the verse gives. The Teacher says a man seldom considers his days "…because God keeps him occupied with the joy of his heart." (Ecclesiastes 5:20) The thing keeping him busy is joy. No ledger in sight.
